questions.question: Which three properties define an equivalence relation?
questions.explanation: An equivalence relation is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive.
questions.source_support: Definition: reflexive, symmetric, and transitive.
questions.polish_notes: Quality round 9: rebalanced correct-answer positions to remove option-index guessing cue
questions.skill_detail: Recall the definition of equivalence relation.
option_explanations: Injective/surjective/bijective are properties of functions, not relations.
Finite/countable/uncountable are cardinality terms.

Associativity and distributivity are axioms for binary operations, and diagonalizability is a property of matrices, whereas an equivalence relation is a binary relation required to satisfy $a\sim a$, symmetry $a\sim b\Rightarrow b\sim a$, and transitivity $a\sim b,b\sim c\Rightarrow a\sim c$.

questions.question: For an equivalence relation, any two equivalence classes are either:
questions.explanation: Two equivalence classes are either identical or disjoint — they cannot partially overlap.
questions.skill_detail: equivalence classes are equal or disjoint
questions.source_support: Classes: equal or disjoint.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).
option_explanations: They can be identical, so not always disjoint.
Distinct classes are disjoint, never overlapping.
Distinct classes are disjoint, not always identical.

questions.question: If $a\sim b$ under an equivalence relation, then the classes $[a]$ and $[b]$ are:
questions.explanation: If $a\sim b$, then $[a]=[b]$: related elements generate the same class.
questions.source_support: $a\sim b\iff[a]=[b]$.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).
option_explanations: They are equal, not different.
They coincide, so they are not disjoint.
They are equal, not nested-but-unequal.

questions.question: Under an equivalence relation on $A$, each element of $A$ belongs to:
questions.explanation: Equivalence classes partition the set, so each element belongs to exactly one class.
questions.skill_detail: each element lies in exactly one class
questions.source_support: Each element in exactly one class.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).
option_explanations: Classes are disjoint, so an element is in exactly one, not at least two.
It is in one class, not every class.
Reflexivity puts each element in its own class, so not zero.

questions.question: What is the interpretation of an equivalence relation?
options: It counts the number of elements in a set
It orders objects from smallest to largest
It says when different objects count as the same
questions.explanation: An equivalence relation formalizes when different objects should be treated as the same for a particular purpose.
questions.source_support: Interpretation: it formalizes when different objects should be treated as the same for a particular purpose.
option_explanations: It does not count elements.
Ordering smallest to largest is an order relation, not equivalence.
It does not define matrix multiplication.

questions.question: On the integers, the relation “has the same parity as” is an equivalence relation. Which property explains why every integer has the same parity as itself?
questions.explanation: Reflexivity is the property $a\sim a$, which is why every integer has the same parity as itself.
questions.source_support: Definition: reflexive means a ~ a.
questions.polish_notes: Quality round 9: rebalanced correct-answer positions to remove option-index guessing cue
option_explanations: Transitivity is $a\sim b,\,b\sim c\Rightarrow a\sim c$.
Symmetry is $a\sim b\Rightarrow b\sim a$.
Surjectivity is a function property, not a relation property.

options: Yes, because $4$ and $10$ have the same remainder modulo $3$
No, because congruence modulo $3$ is not an equivalence relation
Yes, because all integers are congruent modulo $3$

questions.source_support: Example: congruence modulo n is an equivalence relation on integers.

Not all integers are congruent mod $3$.

questions.question: Which relation on real numbers is not an equivalence relation?
questions.explanation: $a<b$ is not an equivalence relation because it is not reflexive or symmetric (e.g. $a<a$ fails).
questions.source_support: Definition requires reflexive, symmetric, and transitive.

'$a-b$ is an integer' is an equivalence relation.
$|a|=|b|$ is an equivalence relation.

questions.question: Equal cardinality of sets is an equivalence relation. What proves the symmetric part?
options: The empty set has one element
The inverse of a bijection is a bijection
Every set has larger power set
questions.explanation: Symmetry of 'equal cardinality' holds because the inverse of a bijection $A\to B$ is a bijection $B\to A$.

questions.question: If $a\sim b$ and $b\sim c$ imply $a\sim c$, which property is being used?
questions.explanation: $a\sim b$ and $b\sim c\Rightarrow a\sim c$ is exactly transitivity.
questions.source_support: Definition: transitive means if a ~ b and b ~ c, then a ~ c.
questions.skill_detail: Name a defining property from its implication.
option_explanations: Reflexivity is $a\sim a$.
Symmetry is $a\sim b\Rightarrow b\sim a$.
Commutativity is not a relation property.

questions.question: Why is symmetry not the same as reflexivity?
options: Reflexivity says every relation can be reversed
Symmetry is between two objects; reflexivity is an object with itself
The two words always describe identical conditions, which is false
Symmetry says every object is related to itself
questions.explanation: Symmetry reverses a relation between two distinct objects ($a\sim b\Rightarrow b\sim a$), while reflexivity relates each object to itself ($a\sim a$).
questions.source_support: Definition lists reflexive and symmetric as separate conditions.
questions.polish_notes: Quality round 9: rebalanced correct-answer positions to remove option-index guessing cue
option_explanations: Reflexivity is not about reversing relations.
They are different conditions, not identical.
'Every object related to itself' is reflexivity, not symmetry.

questions.question: Why is transitivity important when equivalence is meant to represent “same for this purpose”?
options: It prevents chains of sameness from breaking at the endpoints
It says unrelated objects must become related
It forces every equivalence class to contain one element
It says $a\sim b$ can hold only when $a=b$
questions.explanation: Transitivity keeps chains of sameness intact: if each link is 'same', the endpoints are 'same' too.
questions.source_support: Definition: transitive means if a ~ b and b ~ c, then a ~ c.
option_explanations: Transitivity applies only after both $a\sim b$ and $b\sim c$ are known; it does not create a relation between previously unrelated objects.
An equivalence class can contain many elements, such as all integers with the same remainder modulo a fixed number. Transitivity does not force singleton classes.
Equivalent objects may be distinct; congruent integers give standard examples. This choice confuses being treated as the same for one purpose with literal equality.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).

Sets with equal cardinality must contain exactly the same elements
Equal cardinality means both sets are finite
Equal cardinality gives a linear order of all sets
questions.explanation: Sets with a bijection between them are treated as having the same size, which is the equivalence 'equal cardinality'.
questions.source_support: Relevant result: equal cardinality is an equivalence relation on sets.

option_explanations: Equal cardinality does not require the same elements.
It applies to infinite sets too, not only finite ones.
It does not impose a linear order on sets.

questions.question: Under congruence modulo $4$, which numbers lie in the same equivalence class as $1$?
questions.explanation: Mod $4$, $1\equiv5\equiv-3$ (each leaves remainder $1$), so $5$ and $-3$ share the class of $1$.
questions.source_support: Example: congruence modulo n is an equivalence relation on integers.
questions.skill_detail: Find members of a congruence class.
option_explanations: $2$ and $6$ are $\equiv2\pmod4$, not $1$.
$3$ and $7$ are $\equiv3\pmod4$, not $1$.
$0$ and $4$ are $\equiv0\pmod4$, not $1$.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).

questions.question: A relation satisfies reflexivity and symmetry, but there are $a,b,c$ with $a\sim b$ and $b\sim c$ while $a\not\sim c$. What can be concluded?
options: It is not an equivalence relation because transitivity fails
It is an equivalence relation because two properties are enough
questions.explanation: Reflexivity and symmetry hold, but $a\sim b,\,b\sim c$ with $a\not\sim c$ means transitivity fails, so it is not an equivalence relation.
questions.source_support: Definition requires reflexive, symmetric, and transitive.
questions.skill_detail: Use a failed chain to reject equivalence.
option_explanations: Reflexivity holds, so it does not fail reflexivity.
Symmetry holds, so it does not fail symmetry.
All three properties are required; two are not enough.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).
